Entry: Is she to be buried in Christian burial that wilfully seeks her own salvation?
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: I tell thee she is; and therefore make her grave straight: the crowner hath sat on her and finds it Christian burial.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: How can that be unless she drowned herself in her own defence?
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Why 'tis found so.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: It must be se offendendo; it cannot be else. For here lies the point: if I drown myself wittingly it argues an act: and an act hath three branches—it is to act to do to perform: argal she drowned herself wittingly.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Nay but hear you Goodman Delver—
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: Give me leave. Here lies the water; good: here stands the man; good: if the man go to this water and drown himself, good: or if he come to the water and drown himself, good: but if the water come to him and drown him he drowns not himself: argal he that is not guilty of his own death shortens not his own life.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: But is this law?
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: Ay marry is't—crowner's quest law.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Will you ha' the truth on't? If this had not been a gentlewoman she should have been buried out o' Christian burial.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: Why there thou say'st: and the more pity that great folk should have countenance in this world to drown or hang themselves more than their even Christian. Come, my spade.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Go to.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: What is he that builds stronger than either the mason the shipwright or the carpenter?
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: The gallows-maker; for that frame outlives a thousand tenants.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: I like thy wit well in good faith: the gallows does well; but how does it well? it does well to those that do ill: now thou dost ill to say the gallows is built stronger than the church: argal the gallows may do well to thee.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Who builds stronger than a mason a shipwright or a carpenter?
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: Ay tell me that and unyoke.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Marry now I can tell.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: To't.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Mass I cannot tell.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: Cudgel thy brains no more about it for your dull ass will not mend his pace with beating; and when you are asked this question next say 'a grave-maker:' the houses that he makes last till doomsday.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Go get thee to Yaughan; fetch me a stoup of liquor.
Speaker: Second Clown

Entry: In youth when I did love did love methought it was very sweet; To contract O the time for ah my behove methought there was nothing meet.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Has this fellow no feeling of his business that he sings at grave-making?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Custom hath made it in him a property of easiness.
Speaker: Horatio

Entry: 'Tis e'en so: the hand of little employment hath the daintier sense.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: But age with his stealing steps hath clawed me in his clutch; And hath shipped me intil the land as if I had never been such.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: That skull had a tongue in it and could sing once: how the knave jowls it to the ground as if it were Cain's jaw-bone that did the first murder!
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: It might be the pate of a politician which this ass now o'erreaches; one that would circumvent God might it not?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: It might my lord.
Speaker: Horatio

Entry: Or of a courtier which could say 'Good morrow sweet lord! How dost thou sweet lord?' This might be my lord such-a-one that praised my lord such-a-one's horse when he meant to beg it—might it not?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Ay my lord.
Speaker: Horatio

Entry: Why e'en so: and now my Lady Worm's chapless and knocked about the mazard with a sexton's spade: here's fine revolution an we had the trick to see't.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Did these bones cost no more the breeding but to play at loggats with 'em? mine ache to think on't.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: A pick-axe and a spade a spade; For and a shrouding sheet: O a pit of clay for to be made For such a guest is meet.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: There's another: why may not that be the skull of a lawyer? Where be his quiddits now his quillets his cases his tenures and his tricks?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: What's that his honour?
Speaker: Horatio

Entry: Is not this something more than fantasy? Think on that.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Here lies the water; good: here stands the man; good: if the man go to this water and drown himself—
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: This doth well for these—but what of this man's picture? Look you.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: The very conveyances of his lands will hardly lie in this box; and must the inheritor himself have no more, ha?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Not a jot more my lord.
Speaker: Horatio

Entry: Is not parchment made of sheep-skins?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Ay my lord And of calves-skins too.
Speaker: Horatio

Entry: Those are sheep and calves which seek out assurance in that. I will speak to this fellow.—Whose grave's this sirrah?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Mine sir.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: I think it be thine indeed; for thou liest in't.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: You lie out on't sir and therefore it is not yours: for my part I do not lie in't.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: 'Tis a quick lie sir; 'twill away gain from me to you.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: What man dost thou dig it for?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: For no man madam.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: What woman then?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: For none neither.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Who is to be buried in't?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: One that was a woman sir; but rest her soul she's dead.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: How absolute the knave is! we must speak by the card or equivocation will undo us.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: By the Lord Horatio these three years I have taken note of it; the age is grown so picked that the toe of the peasant comes so near the heel of the courtier he galls his kibe.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: How long hast thou been a grave-maker?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Of all the days i' the year I came to't that day that our last king Hamlet o'ercame Fortinbras.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: How long is that since?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Cannot you tell that? every fool can tell that: it was the very day that young Hamlet was born—
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: I' faith if he be not rotten before he die—
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Ha! ha! ha!—
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: —we shall have him a piece of a carrion: Lord an he had lain i' the ground two years he would not have smelled.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: How came he mad?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Very strangely by a kind of madness.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Of what?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Why here in Denmark: I have been sexton here man and boy thirty years.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: How long will a man lie i' the earth ere he rot?
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Faith if he be not rotten before he die—and we have many pocky corses now-a-days that will scarce hold the laying in—
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: He must build churches then.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: No I tell thee he will keep no mean in the talking to himself: words words words.
Speaker: First Clown

Entry: Alas poor Yorick! I knew him Horatio: a fellow of infinite jest of most excellent fancy.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: He hath borne me on his back a thousand times; and now how abhorred in my imagination it is!
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: My gorge rises at it. Here hung those lips that I have kissed I know not how oft.
Speaker: Hamlet

Entry: Where be your gibes now? your gambols? your songs? your flashes of merriment that were wont to set the table on a roar?
Speaker: Hamlet
